# AF 第五章 原文（重制基线）

## Chapter 5

[P01] As winter drew on, Mollie became more and more troublesome（麻烦的）. She was late for work every morning and said she had overslept（睡过头） to excuse herself, and she complained of strange pains, although she ate very well. On every kind of pretext（借口） she would run away from work and go to the drinking pool, where she would stand foolishly looking at her own reflection（反思） in the water. But there were also rumours（谣言） of something more serious. One day, as Mollie walked happily into the yard, moving her long tail about and chewing（咀嚼） a stalk（茎） of hay（干草）, Clover took her aside（旁边）. "Mollie," she said, "I have something very serious to say to you.

[P02] This morning I saw you looking over the hedge（树篱） that divides Animal Farm from Foxwood（狐林）. One of Mr. Pilkington's men stood on the other side of the hedge. And--I was a long way away, but I am almost certain I saw this--he talked to you and you let him stroke your nose. What does that mean, Mollie?""He didn't（没有）! I wasn't（不是）! It isn't（不是） true!" cried Mollie, starting to prance（欢跃） about and paw（爪子） the ground."Mollie! Look me in the face. Do you give me your word of honour that that man did not stroke your nose?""It isn't true!" repeated Mollie, but she could not look Clover in the face, and the next moment she took to her heels（脚跟） and galloped（疾驰） away into the field. A thought struck（打击） Clover.

[P03] Without telling the others, she went to Mollie's stall（畜栏） and turned over the straw（稻草） with her hoof（蹄）. Hidden under the straw was a little pile of lump（块） sugar and several bunches（束） of ribbon（丝带） of different colours. A thought struck Clover. Three days later Mollie disappeared. For some weeks no one knew where she was. Then the pigeons reported they had seen her on the other side of Willingdon. She was between the shafts（车辕） of a smart dogcart（狗车） painted red and black, standing outside a public-house. A fat red-faced man in check breeches（马裤） and gaiters（绑腿）, who looked like a publican（酒馆老板）, was stroking her nose and feeding her sugar.

[P04] Her coat was newly clipped（修剪） and she wore a scarlet（猩红色） ribbon round her forelock（额发）. She seemed to be enjoying herself, so the pigeons said. None of the animals ever spoke of Mollie again. In January came bitterly hard weather. The earth was like iron, and nothing could be done in the fields. Many meetings were held in the big barn（谷仓）, and the pigs kept themselves busy planning the work of the coming season. It had come to be accepted that the pigs, who were clearly cleverer than the other animals, should decide all questions of farm policy（政策）, though their decisions had to be agreed by a majority（大多数） vote.

[P05] This arrangement（安排） would have worked well if not for the quarrels（争吵） between Snowball and Napoleon. These two disagreed（不同意） at every point possible. If one suggested sowing（播种） more barley（大麦）, the other demanded（要求） more oats（燕麦）, and if one said a field was right for cabbages, the other declared（宣布） it useless（无用） except for roots. Each had his own followers（追随者）, and there were wild debates. At the Meetings Snowball often won the majority by his brilliant（聪明的） speeches, but Napoleon was better at gathering（聚集） support in between times.

[P06] He was especially good with the sheep. Lately the sheep had started bleating "Four legs good, two legs bad" at any time, and they often broke into the Meeting with this. They were especially likely to burst（爆发） out this at big moments in Snowball's speeches. Snowball had studied some old copies of the 'Farmer and Stockbreeder（饲养员）' he had found in the farmhouse（农舍）, and was full of plans for new ideas. He talked with learning about field drains（排水沟）, silage（青贮饲料）, and basic slag（矿渣）, and had worked out a complex（复杂的） plan for all the animals to drop their dung（粪便） right in the fields, at a different spot（地点） every day, to save the labour（劳作） of carting it away.

[P07] Napoleon came up with no plans of his own, but said quietly that Snowball's plans would come to nothing, and he seemed to be waiting for his own moment to act. But of all their arguments（争论）, none was so bitter as the one that took place over the windmill（风车）. These two disagreed at every single point where disagreement（分歧） was possible. In the long pasture（牧场）, not far from the farm buildings, there stood a small hill, which was the highest point on the whole farm.

[P08] After looking at the ground, Snowball said that this was just the place for a windmill, which could be made to run a dynamo（发电机） and give the farm electrical（电力的） power. This would light the stalls（畜栏） and warm them in winter, and would also run a circular（圆形的） saw, a chaff（谷壳）-cutter（切割机）, a mangel（饲料甜菜）-slicer, and an electric milking machine. The animals had never heard of anything of this kind before (for the farm was an old-fashioned one and had only the most simple machinery（机器）), and they listened in surprise while Snowball called up pictures of wonderful machines which would do their work for them while they ate grass at their ease in the fields or improved their minds with reading and talking. Within a few weeks Snowball's plans for the windmill were fully worked out.

[P09] The mechanical（机械的） details came mostly from three books that had belonged to Mr. Jones—'One Thousand Useful Things to Do About the House', 'Every Man His Own Bricklayer（砖匠）', and 'Electricity for Beginners（初学者）'. Snowball used as his study a shed that had once been used for incubators（孵化器） and had a smooth wooden floor, good for drawing on. He shut himself in there for hours. With his books held open by a stone, and with a piece of chalk gripped（攫住） between the knuckles（指关节） of his trotter（猪蹄）, he would move quickly to and fro（来回）, drawing line after line and making little whimpers（呜咽） of excitement. Gradually the plans grew into a complicated（复杂的） mass（大量） of cranks（曲柄） and cog（齿轮）-wheels, covering more than half the floor, which the other animals found impossible to understand but very impressive（令人印象深刻）.

[P10] All of them came to look at Snowball's drawings at least once a day. Even the hens and ducks came, and tried hard not to step on the chalk marks. Only Napoleon kept away. He had spoken against the windmill from the start. One day, however, he came without warning to look at the plans. He walked heavily（沉重地） round the shed, looked closely at every detail and snuffed（嗅） at them once or twice, then stood for a little while watching them out of the corner of his eye; then suddenly he lifted his leg, made water over the plans, and walked out without saying a word.

[P11] Snowball did not deny that to build it would be a hard job. Stone would have to be carried and built into walls, then the sails made, and after that dynamos（发电机） and cables（电缆）. (How these were to be got, Snowball did not say.) But he said it could all be done in a year. And after that, he declared, so much labour（劳作） would be saved that the animals would only need to work three days a week. Napoleon argued that the great need was to increase food production, and that if they wasted time on the windmill they would all starve（饿死） to death.

[P12] The animals divided themselves into two groups, each with its own slogan: "Vote for Snowball and the three-day week" and "Vote for Napoleon and the full manger（食槽）." Benjamin was the only animal who did not take either side. He refused to believe that food would become more plentiful（丰富）, and he refused to believe that the windmill would save work. Windmill or no windmill, he said, life would go on just as it had always gone on—that is, badly.

[P13] Jones. They had even more reason to do this because the news of their defeat had spread across the countryside and made the animals on the neighbouring farms more restless（不安） than ever. As usual, Snowball and Napoleon did not agree. According to Napoleon, the animals must get guns and train to use them. According to Snowball, they must send out more and more pigeons and stir up uprising among the animals on the other farms. One argued that if they could not defend（保卫） themselves they would surely be conquered（征服）, the other argued that if rebellions（叛乱） broke out everywhere they would not need to defend themselves.

[P14] The animals listened first to Napoleon, and then to Snowball, and they could not make up their minds which one was right; indeed, they always found themselves agreeing with the one who was speaking at that moment, and at last the day came when Snowball's plans were completed. At last the day came when Snowball's plans were completed. At the Meeting on the following Sunday, the question of whether or not to begin work on the windmill was to be put to the vote. When the animals had gathered（聚集） in the big barn, Snowball stood up and, though now and then bleatingfrom the sheep interrupted（打断） him, he set out his reasons for wanting to build the windmill.

[P15] Then Napoleon stood up to reply. He said quietly that the windmill was nonsense（胡说） and that he told nobody to vote for it, then sat down; he had spoken for only thirty seconds and seemed cold about the effect. At this Snowball jumped up and, shouting down the sheep who had begun bleatingagain, made a hot appeal（呼吁） for the windmill. Until now the animals had been equally divided, but in a moment Snowball's eloquence（口才） carried them away. In bright sentences he painted Animal Farm as it might be when sordid（肮脏） labour（劳作） was lifted from the animals' backs.

[P16] His imagination had now run far beyond chaff-cutters（切割机） and turnip（萝卜）-slicers（切片机）. Electricity, he said, could work threshing（打谷） machines, ploughs, harrows（耙）, rollers（滚筒）, and reapers（收割机） and binders（捆扎机）, and also give every stall its own electric light, hot and cold water, and an electric heater. By the time he finished speaking, there was no doubt which way the vote would go. But just then Napoleon stood up and, throwing a strange sidelong（斜眼） look at Snowball, let out a high-pitched（投掷） whimper（呜咽） of a kind no one had ever heard him make before. At this there was a terrible baying（吠叫） sound outside, and nine huge dogs with brass（黄铜）-studded（镶嵌） collars（项圈） came jumping into the barn.

[P17] They rushed straight at Snowball, who only jumped from his place just in time to escape their snapping（猛咬） jaws（嘴）. In a moment he was out of the door and they were after him. Too amazed and frightened to speak, all the animals crowded through the door to watch the chase（追逐）. Snowball was racing across the long pasture that led to the road. He was running as only a pig can run, but the dogs were close on his heels. Suddenly he slipped（滑倒） and it seemed certain that they had him. Then he was up again, running faster than ever, then the dogs were gaining on him again. One of them almost closed his jaws on Snowball's tail, but Snowball whisked（迅速移） it free just in time.

[P18] Then he put on an extra（额外） spurt（冲刺） and, with only a few inches to spare, slipped through a hole in the hedge, and after that he was seen no more. Silent and terrified（恐惧）, the animals crept（爬行） back into the barn. In a moment the dogs came bounding（跳跃） back. At first no one had been able to imagine where these creatures（生物） came from, but the problem was soon solved: they were the puppies whom Napoleon had taken away from their mothers and reared（用后腿站立） privately.

[P19] Though not yet fully grown, they were huge dogs, and looked as fierce as wolves. They stayed close to Napoleon. People noticed that they wagged（摇摆） their tails to him just as the other dogs had once done to Mr. Jones. Napoleon, with the dogs following him, now climbed onto the raised part of the floor where Major had stood before to give his speech. He announced that from now on the Sunday-morning Meetings would end. They were unnecessary（不必要的）, he said, and wasted time. In future all questions about the running of the farm would be settled by a special committee（委员会） of pigs, led by himself.

[P20] These would meet in private and later tell the others their decisions. In spite of the shock that Snowball's expulsion had given them, the animals were dismayed by this announcement. Although Snowball's expulsion（驱逐） had shocked them, the animals were dismayed（沮丧） by this announcement（宣布）. Several of them would have protested（抗议） if they could have found the right arguments. Even Boxer was vaguely（含糊地） troubled. He set his ears back, shook his forelock several times, and tried hard to marshal（元帅） his thoughts; but in the end he could not think of anything to say.

[P21] Some of the pigs themselves, however, were more articulate（能说会道的）. Four young porkers（肉猪） in the front row uttered（说出） shrill（尖锐的） squeals（尖叫） of disapproval（不赞成）, and all four of them sprang（跳起） to their feet and began speaking at once. But suddenly the dogs sitting round Napoleon let out deep, menacing（威胁的） growls（咆哮）, and the pigs fell silent and sat down again. Then the sheep broke out into a tremendous（极大的） bleating of "Four legs good, two legs bad!" which went on for nearly a quarter of an hour and put an end to any chance of discussion.

[P22] Do not imagine, comrades（同志们）, that leadership（领导） is a pleasure! On the contrary（相反的）, it is a deep and heavy responsibility（责任）. No one believes more firmly than Comrade（同志） Napoleon that all animals are equal. He would be happy to let you decide for yourselves. But sometimes you might decide wrong, comrades, and then where should we be? Suppose you had decided to follow Snowball, with his moonshine（空想） of windmills（风车） -- Snowball, who was no better than a criminal（罪犯）?""He fought bravely at the Battle of the Cowshed（牛棚）," said somebody."Bravery（勇敢） is not enough," said Squealer. "Loyalty（忠诚） and obedience（服从） are more important. And as to the Battle of the Cowshed, the time will come when we shall find that Snowball's part in it was much exaggerated（夸大）.

[P23] Discipline（纪律）, comrades, iron discipline! That is the watchword（口号） for today. One false step, and our enemies would be upon us. Surely, comrades, you do not want Jones back?" Once again this argument（争论） was unanswerable（无法回答）. Certainly the animals did not want Jones back; if holding debates on Sunday mornings might bring him back, then the debates must stop. Boxer, who had now had time to think things over, voiced the general feeling by saying: "If Comrade Napoleon says it, it must be right." And from then on he adopted（采用） the maxim（格言）, "Napoleon is always right," in addition to his private motto of "I will work harder." By this time the weather had broken and the spring ploughing had begun.

[P24] The shed where Snowball had drawn his plans of the windmill was now shut up, and everyone supposed the plans had been rubbed off the floor. Every Sunday morning at ten the animals met in the big barn to get their orders for the week. The skull（头骨） of old Major, now clean of flesh（肉）, had been dug up from the orchard（果园） and placed on a stump（树桩） at the foot of the flagstaff（旗杆）, beside the gun. After the flag was hoisted（升起）, the animals walked past the skull in a reverent（虔诚的） way before entering the barn. These days they did not sit all together as before.

[P25] Napoleon, with Squealer and another pig named Minimus, who was good at making songs and poems, sat on the front of the platform（舞台）, with the nine young dogs in a half-circle round them, and the other pigs behind. The rest of the animals sat facing them in the barn. Napoleon read out the orders for the week in a gruff（粗哑的） soldierly way, and after singing 'animals of England', all the animals went their ways. On the third Sunday after Snowball was driven out, the animals were surprised to hear Napoleon say that the windmill was to be built after all.

[P26] He gave no reason for changing his mind, but warned the animals that this extra task meant very hard work, and it might even be necessary to reduce their rations（配给）. The plans, however, had all been prepared, down to the last detail. A special committee of pigs had worked on them for three weeks. The building of the windmill, with other improvements, would take two years. That evening Squealer explained privately that Napoleon had never really been against the windmill. On the contrary, he had supported it in the beginning, and the plan Snowball had drawn on the floor of the incubator（孵化器） shed had actually been stolen from among Napoleon's papers.

[P27] The windmill was, in fact, Napoleon's own creation. Why, then, asked somebody, had he spoken so strongly against it? Here Squealer looked very sly（狡猾的）. That, he said, was Comrade Napoleon's cunning（狡猾）. He had seemed to oppose the windmill, simply to get rid of Snowball, a dangerous character and a bad influence. Now that Snowball was gone, the plan could go forward without his interference（干涉）. This, said Squealer, was called tactics（策略）. He repeated, "Tactics, comrades, tactics!" skipping（跳跃） round and whisking（搅拌） his tail with a merry（快乐） laugh. The animals were not certain what the word meant, but Squealer spoke so persuasively（有说服力）, and the three dogs with him growled（咆哮） so threateningly（威胁地）, that they accepted his explanation without further（进一步） questions.
